title: Election anxiety is broad, partisan in its targets, and connected to confidence in democratic administration
source_unit: Gallup and Charles F. Kettering Foundation, Election Concerns Run High Ahead of 2026 Midterms, July 29, 2026
geography: United States; adults surveyed ahead of the 2026 congressional and state elections

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the web and mail Democracy for All Project survey

leader_pressure_concern.unit: percent expressing a great deal or fair amount of concern that political leaders could pressure election officials to change outcomes

ballot_handling_concern.unit: percent concerned about ballots being improperly handled, counted, or secured

voter_intimidation_concern.unit: percent concerned about voter intimidation near polling places

multiple_concerns.unit: percent reporting at least a fair amount of concern about multiple aspects of the election process

observations.method: Gallup/Kettering web-and-mail survey of 23,683 U.S. adults fielded April 24-June 10, 2026; published margin of sampling error ±1 percentage point at 95% confidence.
observations.uncertainty: These are perceptions and concerns, not verified election risks or predictions of turnout, fraud, intimidation, or outcome acceptance; the source notes no trend comparison for the measured questions.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults approaching the 2026 midterm elections, with different political identities, media use, race/ethnicity, and attention to politics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Concern can motivate vigilance and participation rather than reduce confidence; the same respondent may be concerned about several risks for different reasons.

observations.period: April 24-June 10, 2026; partisan targets of election concern

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Democracy for All Project survey; subgroup estimates are party-conditioned

leader_pressure_party_gap.value: 77 percent of Democrats versus 56 percent of Republicans concerned about political leaders pressuring election officials

intimidation_party_gap.value: 60 percent of Democrats versus 46 percent of Republicans concerned about voter intimidation near polling places

ballot_security_party_gap.value: 66 percent of Republicans versus 52 percent of Democrats and 54 percent of independents concerned about ballot handling, counting, or security

observations.method: Published Gallup/Kettering party-conditioned comparisons of election-process concerns.
observations.uncertainty: Party differences describe concern targets, not agreement about the underlying facts or stable partisan trends; cross-sectional association does not establish information or political causality.
observations.subgroup: Democrats, Republicans, independents, and adults with distinct interpretations of election administration and political threat.
observations.counterinterpretation: Partisan asymmetry may reflect different lived experiences, elite cues, media environments, or conceptions of election risk; it does not by itself show that one group is more or less committed to elections.

observations.period: April 24-June 10, 2026; social-media use and perceived election risk

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the survey; social-media-use categories are compared descriptively

intimidation_nonuser_to_heavy.unit: percent concerned about voter intimidation among social-media nonusers versus heavy users spending three or more hours per day

ballot_security_nonuser_to_heavy.unit: percent concerned about ballot handling, counting, or security among nonusers versus heavy users

protest_harm_nonuser_to_heavy.unit: percent concerned about peaceful protesters being harmed among nonusers versus heavy users

attention_route.value: social-media intensity is associated with higher reported concern across several democracy-related risks

observations.method: Gallup descriptive cross-tabulation of election and democratic-process concerns by self-reported social-media use.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is observational; social-media intensity may be a proxy for age, political interest, news exposure, ideology, or other factors and does not demonstrate that platforms produced concern.
observations.subgroup: Social-media nonusers, light or moderate users, and heavy users reporting three or more hours per day.
observations.counterinterpretation: People who are already more concerned may seek more political information and social media; greater exposure may also improve awareness rather than simply increase anxiety.

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Democracy for All Project survey

illegal_action_concern.unit: percent concerned about political leaders taking actions they know may be illegal

anonymous_money_concern.unit: percent concerned about wealthy people or organizations making large anonymous political donations

gerrymandering_concern.unit: percent concerned about district boundaries being changed to favor a party or candidate

legitimacy_route.value: election anxiety extends beyond ballot administration into accountability, political finance, representation, and institutional fairness

observations.method: Gallup/Kettering survey estimates of concerns about broader democratic governance and institutional integrity.
observations.uncertainty: Reported concern does not measure actual illegality, anonymous donations, gerrymandering, institutional fairness, or subsequent political action; several items are normatively and politically interpreted.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults with different party identities, race/ethnicity, political attention, and trust in democratic institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: High concern can reflect heightened civic awareness and demand for accountability rather than democratic withdrawal or declining commitment.

related_sources.claim: The parent Democracy for All Project supplies separate national and local democratic-performance and accountability measures.
Gallup's influencer-audience analysis supplies a separate media-to-political-judgment route.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. election-legitimacy route connecting perceived election risks, partisan threat interpretation, social-media intensity, accountability, political finance, representation, and institutional confidence. It is a large cross-sectional survey, not an election-security audit, forecast, turnout estimate, causal media study, or evidence that concern translates into participation or rejection of outcomes.
